name: Lance
summary: A file and table format for AI data: columnar like Parquet, but fast at fetching single rows, with vector and full-text indexes, versions and room for images and video.
intro: Parquet is built for scans: read a few columns of every row. AI workloads also need the opposite. Training samples random rows, search fetches the 10 nearest matches, and a pipeline backfills a new embedding column. Lance is a columnar file format that keeps scans fast but drops Parquet’s row groups, using encodings that let a reader jump straight to one row. Its authors measured this in a 2025 paper, and the project claims around 100× faster random access than Parquet.

On top of the files sits a table format, much like Iceberg or Delta Lake. Rows are grouped into fragments, and each fragment can have several data files that each hold some of its columns, so adding a column means writing new files rather than rewriting old ones. Every commit writes a new manifest in `_versions/`, which gives ACID transactions, time travel, tags and branches. Deletes are recorded in deletion files instead of rewriting data. Indexes are part of the spec and live in `_indices/`: vector indexes such as IVF_PQ and HNSW, full-text search, and scalar indexes such as B-tree and bitmap. Images, audio and video can sit in the same table as blobs, next to their embeddings and labels.
strengths: Random reads of single rows are fast, so shuffled training and search don’t need a separate copy of the data
Vector, full-text and scalar indexes are stored with the table, so search runs on object storage without a separate vector database
Adding or backfilling a column writes only that column’s new files
Versions, tags and branches give reproducible training sets and easy rollbacks
Images, video, audio and embeddings live alongside ordinary columns
limits: Far fewer engines read it than Parquet or Iceberg
Compacting files to remove deleted rows moves rows to new addresses, so every index has to be remapped, and compaction can clash with index updates
Most tooling is Python and Rust; the Spark, Trino and Flink connectors are younger
Built for AI and search data; for plain BI tables, Parquet under Iceberg or Delta Lake is the safer default

story: Around 2021, Chang She and Lei Xu asked why working with embeddings, images and video was still so much harder than working with tables. The standard formats were built for something else. Parquet is designed for scanning columns: its encodings aren’t “sliceable”, so reading one row usually means loading a whole page, which hurts shuffled training, search results and other point lookups. And when one column holds 4 KiB embeddings or whole images, no row group size works well. They decided to start from first principles, setting aside formats like Parquet and WebDataset, and the idea became LanceDB and its open format, Lance.

The first version paired a columnar file with a versioned table. In April 2024 the team announced Lance v2, a new file format, because v1 “still struggles in a number of cases”. In April 2025 a paper by Weston Pace, Chang She, Lei Xu and others measured its approach to random access against Parquet and Arrow.

As AI labs and companies such as Runway, Midjourney, Netflix, Uber and ByteDance adopted it, LanceDB set up formal community governance in November 2025, with a project management committee modelled on the Apache Way. The format moved to its own website (lance.org) and GitHub organization (lance-format), separate from LanceDB’s database.

choices.choice: No row groups; fast single-row reads
choices.why: Row groups force a size trade-off that wide values break. Lance stores large pages per column and uses encodings a reader can jump into, so fetching one row doesn’t mean decoding a whole page.

choices.choice: Encodings are extensions, not part of the reader
choices.why: Adding an encoding to Parquet means changing every reader across many implementations. In Lance v2 encodings are plug-ins, so new ones can arrive without a new file format.

choices.choice: Add columns by writing new files
choices.why: ML pipelines often backfill a new embedding or label column. Each fragment can hold several data files with different columns, so adding a column attaches new files instead of rewriting the table.

choices.choice: Indexes are part of the table
choices.why: Vector, full-text and scalar indexes live in the dataset’s `_indices/` folder and are versioned with it, so search runs straight from object storage without a separate vector database.
